conditions.humanStudies: Observational detoxification reports, follow-up studies, and registered oral Ibogaine withdrawal research.
conditions.sampleSizes: Published studies and registries vary from small cohorts to planned early-phase trial stages; each source needs its own denominator.
conditions.designQuality: Often uncontrolled, selection-biased, and setting-dependent; approved medications remain the essential comparator.
conditions.outcomes: Withdrawal interruption, craving, relapse, retention, adverse events, and functional recovery require separate measurement.
conditions.limitations: Durability, relapse denominator data, missing follow-up, concurrent supports, and adverse-event denominator data remain incomplete.
conditions.safetySignals: Cardiac risk, concurrent substances, withdrawal physiology, electrolyte issues, psychiatric status, and medication interactions.
conditions.notProven: Ibogaine is not proven to cure opioid addiction.
conditions.bestNextSource: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05029401 and peer-reviewed OUD detoxification outcome papers.

studies.design: Prospective observational, single group, no control
studies.population: Adults with opioid dependence (Mexico)
studies.outcome: Withdrawal scores fell ~55% within ~3 days; 15/30 (50%) reported no opioid use at 1 month; gains persisted 3-12 months below the 1-month peak.
studies.notes: No comparison group; self-selected clinic patients; self-reported outcomes.

studies.design: Observational, single group, no control
studies.population: Adults with opioid dependence (New Zealand)
studies.outcome: Significant reductions in addiction-severity (drug use) and depression over 12 months; withdrawal fell immediately after treatment.
studies.notes: One participant died during treatment. Very small sample; partial follow-up; MAPS-funded author (declared COI).

studies.design: Open-label safety study, single group, hospital-monitored
studies.population: Adults with opioid use disorder (Netherlands)
studies.outcome: Average peak QTc prolongation 95 ms; 50% exceeded QTc 500 ms; severe transient ataxia in all; no torsades under monitoring.
studies.notes: Cardiac/cerebellar safety study, not efficacy. Supports the serious cardiac-risk warning.

studies.design: Retrospective case series, non-medical settings
studies.population: People treated for heroin withdrawal
studies.outcome: Withdrawal resolved within 24h in 25/33, sustained over 72h.
studies.notes: One fatality (possible concurrent heroin use). No medical monitoring; earliest systematic series.

conditions.studiesNote: Small, uncontrolled or open-label studies only; no published randomized placebo-controlled trial. Verified against PubMed.

conditions.humanStudies: FDA allowed an early phase U.S. Noribogaine hydrochloride study to proceed after an IND submission in April 2026.
conditions.sampleSizes: Phase I details should be read from the posted protocol or registry when available.
conditions.designQuality: Phase I permission is safety-focused and does not establish efficacy.
conditions.outcomes: Relapse, craving, safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and retention need controlled data.
conditions.limitations: Noribogaine, Ibogaine, plant Iboga, alcohol-withdrawal risk, and clinic claims are separate subjects.
conditions.safetySignals: Alcohol withdrawal, liver health, medications, QT/QTc, electrolytes, and monitoring requirements.
conditions.notProven: Noribogaine is not FDA-approved for alcohol use disorder.
conditions.bestNextSource: FDA April 24, 2026 announcement and the eventual trial registry entry.

studies.design: Prospective observational cohort (uncontrolled, single-arm; data collected during standard clinical operations at an ibogaine + 5-MeO-DMT treatment program in Mexico). Ibogaine was co-administered with 5-MeO-DMT, so ibogaine effects cannot be isolated.
studies.population: US Special Operations Forces Veterans; of 86 who completed treatment, 45 met criteria for risky alcohol use at pre-treatment (mean age 44; 100% male; 91% White). Cohort also had PTSD symptoms.
studies.outcome: Significant reduction in alcohol use score from pre-treatment (M=7.2, SD=2.3) to 1 month (M=3.6, SD=3.5), sustained at 6 months (M=4.0, SD=2.9; p<.001, partial eta squared=.617). At 1 month: 24% abstinent, 33% non-risky drinking, 42% risky; at 6 months: 16% abstinent, 31% non-risky drinking, 53% risky (partial relapse over time). Responders vs non-responders differed significantly on PTSD symptom and cognitive change but not demographics.
studies.notes: PMID, journal, year, DOI, design, N, population, and all reported numbers confirmed against the PubMed abstract. Major confound: ibogaine co-administered with 5-MeO-DMT, so no isolated ibogaine effect can be attributed. Uncontrolled, no placebo/comparator, self-selected treatment-seeking veterans, all male, 91% White. Alcohol was a secondary focus alongside PTSD. Conflict of interest: author Martin Polanco affiliated with the commercial treatment program (The Mission Within). No control for regression to the mean or expectancy. Adverse events / cardiac safety not characterized in this report.

studies.journal: Progress in Brain Research (Prog Brain Res)
studies.design: Single case report (N=1) with pre/post resting-state SPECT neuroimaging. Sequential protocol: ibogaine on day 1, vaporized 5-MeO-DMT on day 3, at an inpatient clinic in Mexico; ibogaine effects not isolated.
studies.population: One 31-year-old male military veteran with moderate alcohol use disorder.
studies.outcome: Reported improved mood, cessation of alcohol use, and reduced cravings at 5 days post-treatment, sustained at 1 month, with a partial return to mild alcohol use at 2 months. Post-treatment SPECT showed increased perfusion in bilateral caudate nuclei, left putamen, right insula, and temporal, occipital, and cerebellar regions versus baseline.
studies.notes: PMID, journal, year, DOI, design (case report + SPECT), N=1, and population confirmed against the PubMed abstract. N=1 anecdote; no control, no validated alcohol-use outcome instrument reported. Confounded by 5-MeO-DMT co-administration. Same clinic/program lineage as Armstrong 2023 (author Polanco; Crossroads Treatment Center / The Mission Within). Authors explicitly frame these as isolated findings requiring controlled investigation. The abstract reports weight-based doses, deliberately excluded here per the no-dosing rule. Ibogaine's documented cardiotoxicity (QT prolongation, fatal arrhythmias) was not assessed in this report.

conditions.studiesNote: PMID-verified against PubMed; uncontrolled/open-label human data only, no efficacy RCT of ibogaine.

conditions.humanStudies: A 30-person veteran prospective observational study and later neurophysiology work drew attention and require side-by-side design-limit explanation.
conditions.sampleSizes: The best-known Nature Medicine report involved 30 male special operations veterans.
conditions.designQuality: Open-label observational data can generate hypotheses but cannot establish broad efficacy.
conditions.outcomes: Disability, cognition, PTSD symptoms, depression, anxiety, sleep, and quality of life are separate outcomes.
conditions.limitations: Small sample, male veteran population, Mexico treatment setting, concurrent supports, selection effects, and short follow-up.
conditions.safetySignals: Screening, cardiac monitoring, magnesium context, psychiatric history, and follow-up.
conditions.notProven: Ibogaine is not proven as a general TBI treatment.
conditions.bestNextSource: Nature Medicine 2024 magnesium-Ibogaine veteran study and Nature Mental Health 2025 follow-up.
conditions.studiesNote: PMID-verified against PubMed; uncontrolled/open-label human data only, no efficacy RCT of ibogaine.

conditions.humanStudies: PTSD-related signals often appear within veteran or substance-use populations rather than standalone PTSD trials.
conditions.sampleSizes: Currently tied mainly to small observational cohorts and secondary analyses.
conditions.designQuality: Controlled studies with clear PTSD endpoints and adequate follow-up remain limited.
conditions.outcomes: PTSD symptom scales, sleep, functioning, substance use, depression, and narrative meaning are not the same outcome.
conditions.limitations: Confounding, expectation effects, integration/support differences, psychiatric exclusions, and concurrent interventions.
conditions.safetySignals: Psychiatric destabilization, suicidality screening, medications, acute monitoring, and post-session support.
conditions.notProven: Ibogaine is not proven as a PTSD treatment.
conditions.bestNextSource: Veteran TBI studies and updated psychiatric scoping reviews.

studies.design: Prospective, single-arm, open-label observational study (no control group, no blinding). ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04313712. Magnesium-ibogaine (MISTIC protocol) provided together with complementary treatment modalities.
studies.population: 30 male Special Operations Forces veterans with predominantly mild traumatic brain injury; PTSD was a secondary outcome.
studies.outcome: PTSD was a SECONDARY outcome. Significant improvement on the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 at 1 month after treatment (P<0.001, Cohen's d=2.54). Primary outcome was WHODAS disability (improved immediately, d=0.74, and at 1 month, d=2.20). Depression (MADRS, d=2.80) and anxiety (HAM-A, d=2.13) also improved at 1 month.
studies.followUp: 1 month (PTSD assessed at this secondary timepoint); primary WHODAS outcome assessed immediately post-treatment.
studies.notes: Open-label, uncontrolled, all-male SOF sample limits generalizability and causal inference. Authors report no unexpected or serious adverse events; abstract explicitly notes ibogaine's known association with fatal cardiac arrhythmia, with magnesium co-administration used to mitigate cardiac risk. Three co-authors affiliated with Ambio Life Sciences, an ibogaine treatment provider (Vancouver) - confirmed conflict of interest. Verified against PubMed abstract: journal, 2024 publication, vol 30(2):373-381, n=30, design, and all effect sizes match.

studies.design: Secondary mediation/association analysis of the same 30-person MISTIC cohort (linear mixed models; Mystical Experience Questionnaire MEQ30 and resting-state EEG). Not an independent sample.
studies.population: Same 30 male veterans with traumatic brain injury from repeated blast/combat exposure who underwent magnesium-ibogaine therapy.
studies.outcome: Greater intensity of mystical experience during treatment was associated with larger PTSD reductions immediately (time-by-MEQ30 interaction B=-5.89, p<0.001) and at 1 month (B=-4.45, p=0.007), and with decreased peak alpha frequency at 1 month (B=-0.38, p=0.006). Correlational/mediational only.
studies.notes: Same 30 subjects as Cherian 2024 - adds no new participants and inherits all design limitations (open-label, uncontrolled, all-male). Association/mediation analysis cannot establish that ibogaine causes PTSD improvement. Stanford/VA author group overlapping with the primary MISTIC report. Verified against PubMed abstract: journal vol 395(Pt B):120722, 2025, n=30, all B values and p-values match exactly.

studies.journal: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
studies.design: Secondary multimodal neuroimaging analysis (arterial spin labeling and BOLD fMRI) of the same 30-person MISTIC cohort, before/immediately after treatment and at 1-month. Not an independent sample.
studies.population: Same 30 male SOF veterans who received ibogaine treatment for traumatic brain injury sequelae.
studies.outcome: Exploratory whole-brain imaging study, not a PTSD efficacy endpoint. Treatment-induced regional cerebral blood flow changes in the left insula and left anterior cingulate cortex correlated significantly with improvements in TBI-related disability; gradual rCBF increases in cortical, limbic, and striatal subregions plus widespread functional-connectivity changes reported.
studies.notes: Hypothesis-generating, uncontrolled imaging of the same 30-subject open-label cohort. No PTSD-specific clinical efficacy claim; included only as mechanistic context within the trauma cohort. Authors explicitly call for larger controlled neuroimaging studies. Verified against PubMed abstract: journal, 2026, n=30, left insula/left ACC rCBF finding all match.

studies.design: Retrospective, cross-sectional survey of clinic alumni (no control group, no blinding, no randomization); before-vs-after recall of a 30-day window.
studies.population: 51 of 65 eligible US Special Operations Forces veterans who completed an ibogaine + 5-MeO-DMT program in Mexico, 2017-2019 (mean age 40; 96% male; 92% Caucasian/White; 96% OEF/OIF service).
studies.outcome: Very large retrospective pre-post reductions in PTSD symptoms (p<0.001, d=-3.6), alongside suicidal ideation (d=-1.9), cognitive impairment (d=-2.8), depression (d=-3.7) and anxiety (d=-3.1). Increases in retrospective psychological flexibility (d=2.9) correlated strongly with symptom reductions.
studies.followUp: Retrospective single survey; recall of 30 days before vs 30 days after treatment (no prospective follow-up).
studies.notes: Ibogaine was co-administered with 5-MeO-DMT, so PTSD effects cannot be attributed to ibogaine specifically. Retrospective self-report design highly vulnerable to recall and selection bias (only program completers surveyed). One author affiliated with the Terra Incognita Project. Authors describe findings as preliminary. CORRECTION vs researcher row: 92% are Caucasian/White (the 96% figure cited by the researcher is the OEF/OIF service rate, not the White proportion). Verified against PubMed: journal vol 4, 2020, n=51, PTSD d=-3.6 match.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse
studies.design: Prospective, single-arm, open-label clinical-program evaluation (no control, no blinding); online surveys at four timepoints (baseline, 1, 3, 6 months).
studies.population: 86 trauma-exposed male SOF veterans in an ibogaine + 5-MeO-DMT program in Mexico (mean age 42.88; 100% male; 87.2% White; 89.5% non-Hispanic).
studies.outcome: Significant self-reported PTSD symptom improvement baseline to 1 month (p<0.001, d=0.414), with smaller-to-moderate gains in depression (d=0.275), anxiety (d=0.276), insomnia severity (d=0.351), post-concussive symptoms (d=0.389), satisfaction with life (d=0.371), psychological flexibility (d=0.313) and cognitive functioning (d=0.265); signal of durability to 6 months.
studies.notes: Combined ibogaine + 5-MeO-DMT - PTSD effect not attributable to ibogaine alone. Self-report outcomes, no control arm, treatment-seeking all-male SOF sample. Author affiliations with the Center for Psychedelic Drug Research and Education (Ohio State) and Johns Hopkins; program-evaluation data from a private clinic in Mexico. Authors state controlled research is warranted. Verified against PubMed: journal vol 49(5):587-596, 2023, n=86, PTSD d=0.414 match.

studies.design: Prospective, single-arm, open-label clinical-program evaluation (no control, no blinding) of co-occurring risky alcohol use and PTSD symptoms; assessments at pre-treatment, 1, 3, 6 months.
studies.population: Subset of 45 of 86 SOF veterans meeting risky-alcohol-use criteria at baseline in an ibogaine + 5-MeO-DMT program in Mexico (mean age 44; 100% male; 91% White).
studies.outcome: PTSD was a between-group correlate. Primary focus was alcohol use, which fell significantly from pre-treatment through 6 months (partial eta squared=0.617). Alcohol-use responders (abstinent/non-risky) vs non-responders differed significantly and very largely in PTSD symptom change (p<0.01, d=-3.26) and cognitive functioning change (p<0.01, d=-0.99).
studies.notes: Same Mission Within Mexico cohort (overlaps Davis 2023); ibogaine combined with 5-MeO-DMT, so ibogaine-specific PTSD effect is not isolable. Open-label, uncontrolled, all-male. PTSD is a between-group correlate of alcohol response rather than a controlled efficacy endpoint. Co-author Polanco affiliated with The Mission Within (the treating clinic) - confirmed clinic conflict of interest. PubMed lists publication year 2023, journal Military Psychology vol 36(2):184-191; DOI carries a 2022 stem. Verified: n=45 of 86, PTSD d=-3.26 match.

conditions.humanStudies: Mood improvements appear in some Ibogaine-related observational and veteran studies, usually as secondary outcomes.
conditions.sampleSizes: Small cohorts and case-level reports dominate the public literature.
conditions.designQuality: Depression-specific controlled Ibogaine evidence remains limited.
conditions.outcomes: Depression scale changes, quality of life, suicidality, sleep, and substance-use outcomes must be separated.
conditions.limitations: Expectation effects, concurrent treatment, post-acute recovery, integration, and regression to the mean can affect mood measures.
conditions.safetySignals: Suicidality, bipolar disorder, psychosis risk, serotonergic medications, sleep disruption, and cardiac risk.
conditions.notProven: Ibogaine is not proven as a depression treatment.
conditions.bestNextSource: 2026 psychiatric scoping review and condition-specific controlled trials if they appear.

studies.design: Prospective open-label, single-arm observational study (no control, no blinding); magnesium co-administered (MISTIC protocol); ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04313712
studies.population: 30 male Special Operations Forces veterans with predominantly mild traumatic brain injury; depression was a secondary outcome measured by the Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS)
studies.outcome: Significant improvement in depression at 1 month after a single treatment (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = 2.80); also improvements in PTSD (d = 2.54) and anxiety (d = 2.13) at 1 month. Functioning (WHODAS) was the primary outcome (improved immediately, d = 0.74, and at 1 month, d = 2.20).
studies.followUp: Immediately post-treatment (primary) and 1 month post-treatment (secondary); no longer-term controlled follow-up
studies.notes: PMID confirmed in PubMed; journal/year/design/N/outcome match the abstract exactly. Open-label, no placebo/control arm, small all-male self-selected sample; depression only a secondary outcome. Three authors are affiliated with Ambio Life Sciences (ibogaine treatment provider) — commercial conflict of interest. Abstract reports no unexpected or serious adverse events, but ibogaine carries documented cardiotoxicity (fatal arrhythmia) that magnesium was used to attempt to mitigate. Effect sizes are very large for an uncontrolled design; expectancy/placebo effects uncontrolled. Authors themselves state controlled trials are needed.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse (Am J Drug Alcohol Abuse)
studies.design: Observational 12-month follow-up study, single-arm, no control; single ibogaine treatment by one of two providers in New Zealand
studies.population: 14 opioid-dependent adults (50% female); depression a secondary outcome measured by Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II); primary outcome was addiction severity (ASI-Lite)
studies.outcome: Among the 8 participants completing all interviews, BDI-II scores fell significantly from baseline to 12-month follow-up (P < 0.001); ASI-Lite drug-use composite score also fell significantly (p = 0.002). SOWS withdrawal scores fell acutely in all 14 (p = 0.015).
studies.followUp: 12 months (depression analysis limited to the 8 completers)
studies.notes: PMID confirmed in PubMed; all fields match the abstract exactly. Very small sample, high attrition (8 of 14 completed all interviews), no control group or blinding; depression a secondary endpoint. One enrolled patient DIED during treatment — a direct safety signal stated in the abstract. Co-author Yazar-Klosinski is a salaried MAPS employee (advocacy-funding conflict of interest, explicitly noted in the author affiliation). Confounded by concurrent reduction in opioid use, so mood change cannot be attributed to a direct antidepressant effect.

studies.journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences (Ann N Y Acad Sci)
studies.design: Open-label inpatient detoxification study (pharmacokinetics, safety and preliminary efficacy); single-arm, no control. PubMed indexes the article type as 'Clinical Trial,' but the abstract describes uncontrolled preliminary efficacy measures with no comparison arm.
studies.population: Cocaine- and heroin-dependent persons undergoing inpatient ibogaine detoxification; depressive symptoms assessed by self-report questionnaire (secondary measure)
studies.outcome: Self-reported depressive symptoms were significantly lower after ibogaine treatment and at 30 days after program discharge; craving for cocaine and heroin also significantly decreased.
studies.notes: PMID confirmed in PubMed; journal/year/DOI match. Exact sample size and statistical detail for the depression measure are NOT stated in the abstract (reported only qualitatively as 'significantly lower') — N left null accordingly. No control group or blinding; depression a secondary self-report measure confounded by acute withdrawal/detox. Authors hypothesize aftereffects relate to the metabolite noribogaine. No exact N or follow-up retention figures available from the abstract.

studies.journal: Journal of Psychoactive Drugs (J Psychoactive Drugs)
studies.design: Qualitative collective case study; semi-structured interviews with inductive thematic analysis (no quantitative depression scale, no control)
studies.population: 10 opioid-dependent individuals in New Zealand who used legally prescribed ibogaine for opioid detoxification
studies.outcome: One of seven inductive themes was 'effects of treatment on depression and anxiety'; participants associated treatment with improved mood and reduced anxiety, though relapse occurred in some cases. No quantitative depression outcome was measured.
studies.followUp: Retrospective interviews about post-treatment experience; no defined quantitative follow-up window
studies.notes: PMID confirmed in PubMed; design/population/outcome match the abstract. Qualitative/self-reported lived-experience data only — not a measured depression outcome; subject to recall and selection bias (recruited through ibogaine networks/OST services/snowball sampling). Useful as patient-experience context, not as efficacy evidence. Emphasizes medical screening and post-treatment psychosocial support as critical to positive outcomes.

conditions.humanStudies: Anxiety outcomes are usually measured within TBI, PTSD, or substance-use populations rather than as a standalone indication.
conditions.outcomes: Acute anxiety, generalized anxiety, trauma-linked anxiety, panic symptoms, sleep, and functioning need separate labels.
conditions.limitations: Anxiety can change with withdrawal relief, sleep, expectation, setting, or integration support.
conditions.safetySignals: Acute distress, panic, psychiatric destabilization, benzodiazepines, serotonergic drugs, and cardiac monitoring.
conditions.notProven: Ibogaine is not proven as an anxiety treatment.
conditions.bestNextSource: TBI and psychiatric studies that report anxiety scales.

conditions.humanStudies: A 2026 peer-reviewed case report describes one patient treated with low-dose Ibogaine hydrochloride over 80 days using validated Parkinson's instruments.
conditions.sampleSizes: One published case report in the current public watchlist.
conditions.designQuality: A single case cannot establish efficacy, generalizability, or safety.
conditions.outcomes: Motor symptoms, quality of life, fatigue, mood, sleep, freezing of gait, and adverse events need structured follow-up.
conditions.limitations: One-patient evidence is highly uncertain and vulnerable to placebo, expectation, medication changes, and disease variability.
conditions.safetySignals: Age, cardiac status, neurological comorbidity, drug interactions, sleep worsening, and medication changes.
conditions.notProven: Ibogaine is not proven as a Parkinson's treatment.
conditions.bestNextSource: Journal of Psychedelic Studies 2026 case report via University of Otago.
conditions.studiesNote: No PubMed-indexed clinical study record was found in this dataset. A single repository case report is tracked at low confidence.

conditions.humanStudies: Withdrawal and craving findings appear in OUD studies, observational detoxification reports, and substance-use reviews.
conditions.sampleSizes: Varies by source; each claim needs substance type, timing, and follow-up window.
conditions.designQuality: Acute symptom change is easier to observe than durable relapse prevention.
conditions.outcomes: Withdrawal severity, cravings, time to relapse, treatment retention, and post-acute symptoms must not be merged.
conditions.limitations: Concurrent medications, setting, expectation, follow-up loss, and substance-specific withdrawal risks can change interpretation.
conditions.safetySignals: Withdrawal physiology, dehydration, electrolytes, cardiac risk, benzodiazepines, alcohol, stimulants, opioids, and polysubstance use.
conditions.notProven: Craving reduction or withdrawal relief is not the same as a cure.
conditions.bestNextSource: OUD papers, clinical trial registries, and adverse-event literature.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse
studies.design: Prospective observational study (no control group, no blinding)
studies.population: Adults with DSM-IV opioid dependence (25 male, 5 female) using oxycodone and/or heroin; averaged 3.1 prior treatment episodes
studies.outcome: SOWS scores fell from 31.0 +/- 11.6 pretreatment to 14.0 +/- 9.8 at ~76.5 hours posttreatment (p < 0.001). At 1-month follow-up, 15 of 30 subjects (50%) reported no opioid use in the prior 30 days; Addiction Severity Index drug-use scores improved at all timepoints, maximal at 1 month.
studies.notes: First prospective observational drug-use-outcomes study of ibogaine. Single weight-based oral dose. Open-label, uncontrolled, modest sample, self-reported outcomes. No deaths in this cohort, but design cannot isolate ibogaine's effect from expectancy or co-interventions. Epub 2017; appears in vol 44(1) 2018.

studies.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled single ascending-dose trial (of noribogaine, ibogaine's metabolite)
studies.population: Patients established on methadone opioid substitution therapy seeking to discontinue, switched to morphine the preceding week
studies.outcome: Noribogaine showed only a non-statistically-significant trend toward decreased total opioid-withdrawal score, most notable at the mid dose; study design may have confounded time to resumption of substitution therapy. A concentration-dependent QTc increase was seen (0.17 ms/ng/mL), with largest mean effect of ~16, 28, and 42 ms across ascending dose groups.
studies.followUp: Single-dose study with pharmacokinetic sampling (mean t1/2 ~24-30 h); no long-term follow-up
studies.notes: The ONLY randomized placebo-controlled human study in this set, and it is of the METABOLITE noribogaine, not ibogaine. Did NOT demonstrate significant withdrawal benefit. Dose-dependent QTc prolongation is the headline safety finding. Multiple authors affiliated with DemeRx, Inc. (commercial sponsor) and cardiac-analytics/CRO firms (iCardiac) - clear conflict of interest.

studies.design: Open-label case series with inpatient medical monitoring (no control group)
studies.population: Volunteers seeking detoxification from opioids or cocaine; inpatient setting (St. Kitts)
studies.outcome: Reported that a single dose diminished opioid withdrawal symptoms and reduced drug cravings on multi-dimensional craving questionnaires, with no significant adverse events at the doses used in this study. One-month follow-up data (where available) suggested craving effects persisted.
studies.notes: Largest human case series, but uncontrolled and open-label. Lead author Deborah Mash is commercially linked to ibogaine/noribogaine development (DemeRx) - major conflict of interest. The authors' 'no significant adverse events' claim is specific to this single monitored cohort and contrasts with the broader literature's documented QTc events and deaths; it is not generalizable safety evidence.

studies.design: Retrospective observational study (clinic chart data, no control group)
studies.population: Participants with opioid use disorder undergoing a week-long ibogaine detoxification protocol at a Tijuana, Mexico clinic
studies.outcome: At 48 hours post-administration, withdrawal and craving scores were significantly lower than baseline: 78% showed no objective clinical signs of withdrawal (COWS), 79% reported minimal cravings, and 68% reported subjective withdrawal symptoms only in the mild range (SOWS, BSCS).
studies.notes: Retrospective (MeSH-indexed Retrospective Studies) and uncontrolled; acute (48 h) outcomes only, so no durability data. Two of three authors affiliated with Crossroads Treatment Center (the commercial clinic providing treatment) - conflict of interest. Authors explicitly call for rigorous controlled trials.

studies.design: Descriptive open-label observational safety study (university medical center)
studies.population: Patients with opioid use disorder on maintenance treatment, converted to morphine-sulphate, who had failed to reach abstinence with standard care
studies.outcome: Primary focus was safety: mean maximum QTc (Fridericia) prolongation of 95 ms (range 29-146 ms); 50% reached QTc > 500 ms; in 6 of 14, prolongation > 450 ms lasted beyond 24 h. Severe transient ataxia (unable to walk unaided) occurred in ALL patients. No torsades de pointes observed. Withdrawal/psychomimetic effects were mostly tolerable - 11 of 14 did not return to morphine within 24 h.
studies.followUp: At least 24 hours of intensive monitoring
studies.notes: Most rigorous safety characterization in a hospital setting. Single weight-based dose. Foregrounds the cardiac (QTc > 500 ms, bradycardia) and cerebellar (universal severe ataxia) harms. No torsades or deaths in this small monitored cohort, but the QTc findings substantiate the field's mortality concern. Independent academic group (Radboud UMC / NISPA, Netherlands), no obvious commercial COI.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse
studies.design: Longitudinal observational study (no control group)
studies.population: Individuals receiving legal ibogaine treatment for opioid dependence in New Zealand (50% female)
studies.outcome: Significant acute reduction in SOWS scores immediately after treatment for all participants (n=14, p=0.015). Among completers (n=8), Addiction Severity Index-Lite drug-use composite (p=0.002) and Beck Depression Inventory-II scores (p<0.001) were significantly reduced at 12 months.
studies.notes: Single ibogaine treatment. Small (n=14, only 8 completers), uncontrolled, self-report-based. ONE PATIENT DIED DURING TREATMENT in this cohort - a stark safety signal in a 14-person study. Co-author Yazar-Klosinski is a full-time salaried employee of MAPS - conflict of interest disclosed in the affiliation. Epub 2017; appears in vol 44(1) 2018.

studies.design: Case series, open-label, treatments in non-medical settings (retrospective summary)
studies.population: Heroin-dependent individuals (primarily intravenous use) treated for opioid detoxification
studies.outcome: Resolution of opioid withdrawal signs without further drug-seeking within 24 hours in 25 of 33 patients, sustained through 72 hours of observation. Other outcomes: drug-seeking without withdrawal signs (4), abstinence with attenuated withdrawal signs (2), drug-seeking with continued withdrawal signs (1), and one fatality possibly involving surreptitious heroin use.
studies.notes: Foundational early case series, but treatments occurred in unsupervised non-medical settings and data were summarized retrospectively. Includes ONE FATALITY (possible covert heroin co-use), an early safety signal. Co-author H.S. Lotsof was the ibogaine anti-addiction patent holder/advocate - conflict of interest. Authors explicitly call for systematic clinical investigation. Indexed as Clinical Trial / Journal Article in PubMed.

studies.design: Single forensic case report (autopsy)
studies.population: A heroin-addicted man who self-administered online-purchased iboga (Tabernanthe iboga) extract for detoxification
studies.outcome: Sudden death 5-12 hours after oral ingestion of iboga powder used for detoxification; autopsy showed organ congestion and pulmonary edema, and toxicology found ibogaine plus morphine and codeine. Death attributed probably to ibogaine's cardiovascular effects.
studies.notes: Harm/safety case report, not an efficacy study. Illustrates the lethal cardiac risk of unsupervised, internet-sourced ibogaine used for opioid detoxification, compounded by concurrent opioid use. Included to foreground mortality, not benefit.

conditions.studiesNote: PMID-verified against PubMed; uncontrolled/open-label human data only, no efficacy RCT of ibogaine.
